rationale: A wins because it stays closer to the facts and finds four genuinely usable doors into the story. Its strongest move is "Notion adds enterprise key custody without raising prices, cutting against the security-upsell norm" because that uses a real supplied fact and asks for the missing proof before getting cocky. B can write, but "Notion's compliance stack puts Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive in regulated enterprise" names a competitive fight the update never gave it. That is how a founder ends up pitching a story the proof packet cannot survive.
gaps_in_A: "after it agreed to hand over the keys" is punchy but imprecise. Customers hold their own keys via AWS KMS; Notion did not literally hand keys to banks.

"Notion shipping offline mode in 2026 is an admission the always-online SaaS bet had a ceiling" overstates the confession. The update supports an architecture tension, not an admission unless Notion will say why buyers rejected online-only.
"security-upsell norm" and the "SSO tax" contrast need outside competitor proof. A correctly asks for it, but the angle should not leave the building until that comparison is sourced.
gaps_in_B: "anchored in named institutions" is wrong. The update says four of the five largest US banks run pilots, but no bank is named.
"Confluence and SharePoint on the defensive" invents a named competitive war. The facts do not show displacement, RFP wins, or that Microsoft and Atlassian are newly exposed.
"secure facilities" and "air-gap scenarios" drag the offline angle into unsupported territory. The fact is no-connection editing that syncs on reconnect, not air-gapped deployment.

"pilot-eligible" to "procurement-approvable" is consultant fog. Pilots are not proof of procurement approval, and this category angle mostly repackages the bank and compliance angles with a fancier hat.
